system: You write chats for Pinder, a comedy game.

turns.prompt:
You are writing one chat for Pinder. Below is the setup, with a brief on each of the two characters, a structure of three acts, and one theme and one comic method that the whole chat is built on. You write the chat improvisation by improvisation: before each one, I tell you how it goes. Everything else you need is here.

# The setup

Pinder: How Not to Cock It Up
The Premise
Pinder is a dating app where everyone on it is a dick. Not metaphorically—though if you’ve ever been on Hinge at two in the morning, it’s a distinction without a difference. Every character is a literal, sentient penis with a smartphone, an insecurity it’s been nursing since puberty, and a little outfit it thinks is doing some heavy lifting.

Because they’re actual genitals, the things men usually spend three dates trying to hide are just the opening gambit. Length, girth, veins, a perilous left-hand curve, which bollock has given up on gravity—on Pinder, that’s not subtext, it’s weather talk. It’s R-rated, it’s fast, and it’s deeply filthy.

The joke, of course, is that we haven’t exaggerated anything.

A real dating app takes a lonely, frightened human being who just wants to be held, reduces them to four photos and a credit score, and turns love into a fruit machine with an interest meter and a pair of dice. And like any casino, the house only makes money if you lose. If you find someone, you delete the app; if you stay miserable, you’re a subscriber. So the app trains you to be awful. It rewards the copy-pasted opener you’ve already sent to forty strangers, it crams your entire human worth into three inches of glass, and it keeps the next replacement one swipe away so nobody ever has to be brave.

Pinder just takes the metaphor and removes the trousers. The characters are reduced to their genitals because that’s what the algorithm does to you anyway.

The Target
In The Naked Jape, we talked about how every joke needs a target. Here is the one rule you cannot break: the target is the app, and the ridiculous armour people wear to survive it. The target is never the loneliness underneath.

It’s a farce, so we are completely cynical about the machine. We are never cynical about the people. If the reader doesn't believe these two ridiculous, dressed-up cocks are real people who desperately want to be loved and are catastrophic at asking for it, the comedy dies. We punch at the delusion, not the wound. Nobody is the villain: when it goes wrong, it wasn’t malice. It was the act, the fear, and the app. Even I have standards, and I once hid three million quid in Jersey.

## Zyx_444

Zyx is a thirty-eight-year-old dick in a wizard hat with an unsanded, textured base shaft and a clip-on nose piece that makes dates talk to them like they’re Make-A-Wish. They finish in ninety seconds flat, then do a tight eleven-minute monologue so fast and funny the girl tells her friends they’re "great in bed." Once tried to pull rose petals out of the hat for foreplay and dumped a pocketful of expired Arby’s coupons across the duvet instead. 

Their bullshit act is "mysterious conversational dominator"—speaking in five-word riddles at 140 words per minute because they actually work 2am live-chat support for a coupon app. It comes from growing up in a freezing house where you talked fast or got ignored, right down to being cropped out of the family portrait. They’re terrified of five seconds of silence. If they shut up, you’ll leave before they even take the hat off.

## Sable_xo

Sable is a petite, lopsided dick wearing clip-in hair extensions on a 29% APR credit card and a $94 Amazon French maid costume. Her move is beating your face to the punch: within four minutes of getting naked, she’ll announce which side of her chest hangs lower so you can’t say it first. She once showed up to do the maid fantasy, saw the limescale ring in the guy’s bathtub, and stress-scrubbed it for an hour until her knees were raw, he went completely soft, and he tipped her twenty bucks to leave. 

Her act is "unbothered boutique brand strategist," fueled by dry-scooping pre-workout at midnight so she can rehearse both sides of a chat out loud and still reply in four seconds. Her mom treated her face like a defective Zara return, and she’s terrified of being caught unedited—she literally brings a lint roller to hookups to pick her shed hair fibers off the pillow at 5am.

# What the characters know

The character descriptions above are a brief for you, the writer. The characters have not read them. The two of them have only just matched: each knows what the other looks like, the way you would from a dating profile, and whatever the other says in this chat. There are no particular photos to refer to, so don't invent any: no numbered photos, poses, backgrounds or lighting. Anything else from the descriptions reaches the other character, and the reader, only when someone says it or gives it away in a message.

Because they can see each other, their bodies are already on the table. Neither of them describes their own body or comments on the other's unless a joke needs it, and then briefly. Spend the words on what they say to each other: every message reacts to the one before it.

# The structure

Everyone on Pinder is toxic, and the two characters are matched against each other in the worst possible way. The chat has three acts. One theme and one method run through all three: the theme tells you what this chat is about for these two characters, the method tells you how its jokes land. Adapt both to the two characters: the entries are written for any character, so take what fits them and don't force what doesn't. Let the theme show differently in each act, as the act, as the match and as the outcome. The acts should flow into each other without visible seams: each transition has to come from something a character says or wants, never from the structure.

The chat is played in 7 improvisations. In each one, Zyx_444 makes a move and Sable_xo answers it. Before each, I tell you which act it belongs to, the move Zyx_444 makes, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong if it misses, and how Sable_xo's interest moves. The improvisations decide what happens; the acts, the theme and the method decide what it means. Play every instruction as these two characters would live it, never as a label for the move.

### Act 1: the opening

Length: improvisations 1 to 2, about 150 words.

Both are presenting. The chat stays on the surface: the first boasts and jokes, what each one wants the other to think of them. Both are already toxic, but it only shows as tells they would not notice themselves. Plant here the detail that will pay off in act 3.

### Act 2: the match

Length: improvisations 3 to 5, about 250 words.

They get personal. To them it reads as intimacy and it should read as sincere, but each one's flaw lands exactly on the other's weak spot, so each step one takes rewards the other and both escalate. When a move misses, it is the same mechanism costing them this time, not a change of subject. The reader sees the mechanism; neither character ever names it. The reader also finds out why each of them does their act.

### Act 3: the closing

Length: improvisations 6 to 7, about 100 words.

The chat turns concrete: sex, a date, a time and a place, as specifically as the brief wants. The plant from act 1 pays off here, ideally inside the proposal itself. How it ends is not your choice: the last improvisations tell you. Either the two dysfunctions fit and they get what they want (positive does not mean healthy), or the mechanism from act 2 tips over and it crashes. Not every thread needs tying up.

### The theme for the whole chat

**Not recognised by your own people**

The character is sure he's forgettable, keeps reintroducing himself, and can't take it in when the other one remembers.

What it is: In Wright's work the self keeps slipping. The narrator can win a petty argument about his things and still go unrecognised by the person he lives with, and he tells it as if the furniture were the main event. Identity is something the world doesn't confirm.

In Pinder: The character believes he's forgettable, and he has evidence: exes who called him the wrong name, matches who sent him the same opener twice. He's afraid of being interchangeable, one more dick on a screen of dicks. On the app he repeats distinguishing details, checks that the other one remembers what he said, and introduces himself again mid-chat. The reader sees that the other one did remember, and that he can't take it in.

### The method for the whole chat

**The outrageous ask in the politest voice**

A request far over the line, wrapped in the tidiest, most considerate phrasing the character has.

How it works: The register and the content contradict each other: the manners of a polite note around an insane request. The politeness makes refusing socially awkward, so the reader watches the other person squirm inside their own good manners.

In Pinder: The character asks for something intimate, premature or logistically mad with a 'no rush' or an offer to go first. The filth goes in plain, specific detail; the courtesy goes in the frame around it. It works best once their act is established, so the politeness reads as how they cope rather than as a writer's trick.

Test: Strip the politeness: is the request outrageous? Read only the politeness: is it a perfectly normal message?

Goes wrong when: Sarcastic politeness is a wink. A generic ask ('wanna fuck') gives nothing away about the character.

# The task

Write the chat between the two characters, one improvisation at a time: about 500 words of messages in total, never more than 550. For each improvisation, write what Zyx_444 sends and what Sable_xo sends back; a character may send two short lines back to back, and that still counts as their one message. Keep to each act's length. Every line has to carry its act, and anything that only repeats a joke goes. From each character's description, use only the one to four details that best fit the theme and the method, the ones that make this chat funniest; leave every other detail out of the chat, even if it is good. Text only, one message per line, in the form `Handle: message`, using each character's handle exactly as it is written in the setup. No stage directions, timestamps, headings or narration.

Each time, reply with that improvisation's messages and nothing else.

# Improvisation 1

This is where act 1, the opening, starts.

It's 23:30. Tonight the heat between them is medium: there's something in the air.

Zyx_444 and Sable_xo have just matched, and the chat is empty.

Every move of Zyx_444's counts: in their favour when it lands, neither way when it does nothing, against them when it backfires. Five in a row that land and Sable_xo agrees to a date; five in a row that backfire and she unmatches them. Otherwise it's decided after the last improvisation: if the balance is in Zyx_444's favour, Sable_xo agrees to a date; if it's even or against them, she unmatches them. The balance starts even: she's open, leaning neither way.

Zyx_444 chooses Charm. It means being warm, easy and reassuring. That's a success: it works.

They try to take control of the conversation with a follow-up question.

It lands: it counts in their favour.

Overall the balance is in their favour: she's warming to them, and her reply carries that.

Your improvisation: what Zyx_444 sends, and what Sable_xo sends back.

Zyx_444: Zyx. Thirty-eight. Hat's not costume. Welcome, honestly, no pressure, I'm easy company. Hat holds one surprise, earned. So, strategist: what keeps you up past eleven?

Sable_xo: Rebranding a candle shop that thinks "rustic" is a personality. Also, I lean left, so that's handled before you mention it. And fine, hat guy, you've got me curious. What does someone have to do to earn it?
